text: A shutter speed controls light entering a camera, playing a crucial role in capturing images with the appropriate exposure. It works by allowing varying amounts of light to pass through the camera lens and into the camera sensor. A faster shutter speed, typically measured in fractions of a second, allows less light to enter, preventing overexposure, whereas a slower shutter speed, often in the range of one second to several seconds, allows more light to enter, risking underexposure for moving subjects. Conversely, the aperture adjusts the amount of light entering the camera by controlling the size of the opening in the lens, thereby influencing exposure as well. By default, a wide aperture allows more light in, suitable for capturing action scenes at high speeds, whereas a narrow aperture reduces light, perfect for capturing the detailed and quiet moments in darkness. The interplay of shutter speed and aperture is essential for photographers to achieve the desired exposure and the desired aesthetic in their images.
summary: A shutter speed controls light; aperture adjusts light, fast for action, small for dark.
